sentences.text: The skull, which is 23.7 cm long, has a snout sloping at a 15° angle and features frontal bones forming a rectangular bar between the eye sockets.
Ridges on the skull intersect to create a distinct dagger-shaped protrusion.
The forelimbs included three pectoral vertebrae with rectangular spines, humeri about 24 cm long, and a femur measuring 21.5 cm with one concave edge.
Soft tissue was apparently preserved in the specimen but was removed during preparation.
Workers discovered the holotype near Gronau in northwestern Germany in July 1910 using pickaxes, an event that damaged the pubis of the specimen into 176 pieces.
The type specimen is stored at the University of Münster with the number GPMM A3.B4 and originates from the Isterberg Formation.
A cervical centrum from the Purbeck Group in southern England has a morphology comparable to Brancasaurus, suggesting the taxon may have occurred outside Germany.
Brancasaurus likely preyed on ray-finned fish such as Caturus, Lepidotes, Coelodus, Ionoscopus, and Ainia in surface waters.
Plesiosaurs of the Bückeberg Group, including Brancasaurus, were presumably preserved after sinking to the oxygen-poor bottom of the lake.

The type species is Brancasaurus brancai, named by Wegner in 1914 in honor of the German paleontologist Wilhelm von Branca, and a more recent study by Ketchum and Benson in 2010 assigned it to the family Leptocleididae.
Brancasaurus lived during the Berriasian stage, between 139.1 and 137.05 million years ago, in what is now Germany.
During the deposition of the Wealden 5 and Wealden 6 layers, the lake expanded and became more brackish due to marine transgression.
Researchers found the specimen designated as Gronausaurus was virtually indistinguishable from Brancasaurus, supporting Gronausaurus as a junior synonym.
